title: MODULE 09 — Advanced React, Application Architecture and State Management

overview.text: Module overview
In Module 08, you learned how to build individual React components, manage local state, handle events, create forms, and develop reusable Hooks.
However, building individual components is different from developing a complete application.
Consider a full-featured student dashboard such as PrepSpaces.
A student should be able to:
Navigate between Dashboard, Courses, Learning Progress, Assignments, and Profile.
Open individual course pages and specific lesson pages.
Access information shared between different components.
Maintain authentication while navigating.
Update course progress and immediately see the changes elsewhere.
Load application sections without downloading every page at the beginning.
Recover from component errors without crashing the entire application.
Navigate through a consistent layout.
Use an application that remains responsive as its codebase grows.
These requirements introduce more advanced React concepts.
This module moves beyond individual components and teaches how to design, organize, optimize, and manage complete React applications.
What is advanced React architecture?
Advanced React architecture involves designing how different application parts interact with each other.
It includes:
Component architecture.
State ownership and communication.
Shared and global state.
Routing and navigation.
Authentication-aware interfaces.
Performance optimization.
Lazy loading and code splitting.
Error handling and fallback interfaces.
Feature-based project organization.
A well-designed application should not depend on one enormous component or one global state object containing everything.
Instead, responsibilities should be distributed logically.
How Module 09 connects to previous modules
Module | Main capability
Module 05 — Modern JavaScript | Programming fundamentals
Module 06 — Browser APIs and Asynchronous Programming | Browser and API integration
Module 07 — TypeScript | Type-safe development
Module 08 — React Fundamentals | Reusable interactive components
Module 09 — Advanced React | Complete application architecture, navigation, shared state, and performance
Learning outcomes
By the end of this module, you should be able to:
Explain React's rendering and reconciliation process.
Design reusable component architectures.
Manage communication between distant components.
Implement Context API for shared application state.
Use useMemo and useCallback appropriately.
Manage complex state using useReducer.
Develop reusable custom Hooks.
Implement client-side routing using React Router.
Create nested routes and dynamic route parameters.
Build authentication-aware route interfaces.
Organize layouts and navigation systems.
Implement code splitting and lazy loading.
Handle loading states and component errors.
Optimize application rendering.
Organize large React applications using feature-based architecture.

blocks.text: When developers use React, they describe what the interface should look like using components.
React takes these descriptions and determines how the browser interface should be updated.
When React renders this component, it executes the function and produces a description of the desired interface.
However, rendering a component does not necessarily mean that React must recreate every DOM element.
React can identify which parts of the previous interface are still valid and which need updating.
1.2 The three stages of React updates
React's interface update process can be understood through three stages.
1. Trigger — State update, new props, or another update source
2. Render — React calls components and calculates the next UI description
3. Commit — React applies the necessary changes to the browser DOM
A React component can render initially when it is mounted.
It can render again when relevant state, props, or context changes cause an update.
React calls the component function to calculate what the interface should look like.
The function executes again when React renders the component.
Rendering should be pure: the same props, state, and context should produce the same JSX, and the component should not perform unrelated side effects during rendering.
React applies necessary changes to the browser DOM.
For example, when the counter changes from 0 to 1, React updates the relevant text rather than recreating the entire page.
The browser then paints the updated interface.
React's official documentation describes this sequence as triggering, rendering, and committing. (React)
Reconciliation is the process React uses to determine how the new rendered element tree relates to the previous one.
Therefore, it can update only the necessary DOM content.
This process makes declarative UI updates practical.
React considers element types, positions, and keys when deciding whether component state should be preserved or reset.
Suppose this component appears in a page and the parent renders again.
If the component maintains the same identity in the tree, its state is generally preserved.
However, changing its key can intentionally reset its state.
When userId changes, React treats it as a different component identity.
This is useful when switching between editing sessions, forms, or user-specific views.
Keys are especially important when rendering collections.
Preferred when stable IDs are available:
Imagine that the first course is deleted.
With index-based keys, the remaining courses may receive different identities.
React might associate existing component state with a different course.
Stable keys help React preserve the correct identity when lists change.
When the parent renders, React may also render its child components.
This does not necessarily mean that all those components cause DOM updates.
A re-render is not the same as a full DOM replacement.
Avoid performing these operations during rendering:
These operations can create repeated work and unpredictable behaviour.
Use event handlers, Effects, or other suitable React mechanisms for operations that interact with external systems.

Practical exercise: Create a parent component with three child components. Add state to the parent and observe which components execute during an update. Then experiment with stable keys and changing component identities.

sections.title: Component Composition and Advanced Design Patterns

blocks.text: In Module 08, you learned to create reusable components such as:
In larger applications, component architecture requires more than just separating JSX into files.
Which components should know about application state?
Which components should remain independent of business logic?
These questions introduce advanced component design patterns.
Suppose an application needs multiple card types.
One approach is creating different components for every variation:
Another approach is creating a reusable container that accepts different content.
Now different pages can reuse the same structure:
The parent controls the overall structure, while the child content remains customizable.
A traditional component design pattern distinguishes between two responsibilities.
Responsible for application logic and data.
Primarily responsible for displaying supplied information.
This separation can improve clarity, especially in larger applications.
It is a design guideline rather than a mandatory rule. Modern React components commonly combine data fetching, state and rendering when that produces a simpler design.
Compound components are multiple related components that work together through a shared parent API.

<Tabs>
  <Tabs.List>
    <Tabs.Trigger value="courses">
      Courses
    </Tabs.Trigger>
    <Tabs.Trigger value="progress">
      Progress
    </Tabs.Trigger>
  </Tabs.List>
  <Tabs.Panel value="courses">
    <CourseList />
  </Tabs.Panel>
  <Tabs.Panel value="progress">
    <ProgressOverview />
  </Tabs.Panel>
</Tabs>
The compound components share the same logical context.
This design can make reusable components easier to configure.
A render prop is a function supplied as a component property that determines what content should be rendered.
This can be useful for reusable behaviour that needs customizable rendering.
However, custom Hooks and ordinary component composition often provide simpler alternatives in modern React.
A Higher-Order Component (HOC) is a function that receives a component and returns an enhanced component.
HOCs were widely used to share component behaviour before Hooks became available.
They are still found in some libraries and existing codebases, but custom Hooks are usually simpler for sharing stateful logic within function components.
Container/presentational separation | Separate data handling from presentation
Compound components | Build coordinated component groups
Render props | Customize rendering through callbacks
Higher-Order Components | Enhance or wrap components
Do not use an advanced pattern just because it exists.
Use it when it makes the component API clearer and the application easier to maintain.
Practical exercise: Build a reusable Tabs component using composition and Context. Then create a reusable dashboard Panel using the children prop.
Imagine a dashboard with the following components:

Dashboard
├── SearchBar
├── CourseFilters
└── CourseList
    ├── CourseCard
    ├── CourseCard
    └── CourseCard
The CourseList must display matching courses.
The CourseFilters may also change the displayed results.
How can these components work together?
A common solution is lifting state up.
State lifting means moving shared state from separate child components into their closest common parent.
The parent becomes the single source of truth for that information.
Instead of each child maintaining its own copy, the parent owns the shared state.
CoursePage — Owns search and filter state
SearchBar — Receives search value and callback
CourseFilters — Receives filter value and callback
Now both the search and filter components communicate through the same parent.
React encourages developers to decide which component owns each piece of state.
Modal visibility | Modal owner or its parent
The aim is to avoid keeping duplicated versions of the same data in multiple components.
The official React state-management guidance recommends choosing one owner for each shared piece of state and lifting it to the closest common parent when coordination is required. (React)
State lifting works well when components are close together.
Suppose the App owns the user information, but only UserProfile needs it.
The information must pass through several intermediate components.
It is not always bad, but long chains of unnecessary prop forwarding can make large applications difficult to maintain.
3.6 When to use state lifting and when to use Context
Use state lifting when a small group of related components needs shared information.
Use Context when many components across different levels need access to the same information.
Use a reducer when the shared state has multiple related update operations.
Practical exercise: Build two sibling components that share a selected course. Lift the state to their parent and compare the implementation with an independently managed state approach.
React Context allows information to be made available to components throughout a component tree without manually passing props through every intermediate component.
It is useful for information that many components need to access.

App
├── Navbar
│   └── UserProfile
├── Dashboard
│   ├── WelcomeMessage
│   └── CourseList
└── Footer
Suppose several components need the current user information.
Without Context, you may have to pass the user object through several components.
Context provides a way to share that information directly.
This creates a Context that can carry authentication information.
The Provider makes a value available to descendant components.
The Dashboard and its descendants can access the provided Context.
The useContext() Hook reads the closest matching Context value.
The component does not need to receive user information through every intermediate parent.
In larger applications, Context setup should be separated from individual components.
Now any descendant can use the same authentication interface.
Global state is information that multiple areas of an application need to access.
Selected course tab | Usually local to the course page
Shopping cart | Shared across relevant application pages
An important point: not every state variable belongs in Context.
Putting everything into global state can make the application unnecessarily complicated.
When the value provided by a Context changes, components that consume that Context may render again.
A new object is created whenever the provider renders.
This can make the Context value appear different even when the user itself has not changed.
Keeping local state close to its consumers.
Memoizing provider values when measurement shows a benefit.
Context is a communication mechanism. It is not automatically a complete performance or state-management solution.
The React documentation demonstrates combining Context with reducers to manage more complex screens. (React)
Practical exercise: Create an authentication Context and a theme Context. Use them in the Navbar, Dashboard, Sidebar, and Profile components.
React components may render repeatedly during application interactions.
Sometimes a component performs expensive calculations or passes newly created functions and objects to child components.
Memoization means caching a calculated value or function definition so it can be reused when its dependencies have not changed.
These Hooks are performance optimization tools. They should not be used to make an otherwise incorrect program work.
useMemo caches the result of a calculation between renders when its dependencies remain unchanged.
Here, React can reuse the previous filtered result when neither courses nor search has changed.
Suppose a dashboard processes 100,000 records and calculates statistics.
If this calculation is expensive and runs repeatedly, memoization may help.
It can avoid repeating the calculation when records has not changed.
Using useMemo would add unnecessary complexity.
useCallback caches a function definition between renders.
The handler can retain the same function identity while its dependencies stay unchanged.
React also provides memo() to allow a component to skip rendering when its props have not changed.
A parent component may use useCallback when it needs to pass a stable handler to this memoized component.
This can help avoid unnecessary child renders caused only by a newly created function prop.
memo | Component rendering based on unchanged props
The first caches a calculated value.
If selectedCourse changes, this function can continue reading the value captured by its earlier render.
The dependency array should include reactive values used by the memoized function or calculation.
A common mistake is wrapping every function and value in memoization Hooks.
This can make an application harder to understand.
Identify the expensive component or calculation.

Current React documentation also covers React Compiler, which can automatically handle many memoization optimizations when correctly configured. Consequently, manual useMemo and useCallback should not be applied indiscriminately. (React)
Practical exercise: Create a dashboard with a large course collection. Measure filtering performance, experiment with useMemo, and compare child rendering with and without memo and useCallback.
useState works very well for simple component state.
However, complex application state may require many related update operations.
Managing these operations with many separate state setters can become difficult.
A reducer is a function that receives:
An action describing what should happen.
It should not directly modify its existing state or perform unrelated side effects.
An action describes an event or operation.
Each action has a type property.
Some actions also carry additional information.
Notice that the reducer returns new arrays and objects.
It does not mutate the original state.
The dispatch() function sends an action to the reducer.
React uses the reducer to calculate the next state.
This gives developers one central location for defining state transitions.
Multiple related operations | Can become scattered | Centralized reducer
Update logic | Usually in handlers | In reducer
Action-based updates | Not inherent | Built in
Appropriate for | Local UI state | Complex related state
useReducer is not automatically better than useState.
Choose based on the complexity of the state transitions.
Practical exercise: Build a task-management reducer supporting add, edit, delete, complete, reopen, and priority-change actions.

sections.title: Custom Hooks and Shared Application Logic

blocks.text: 7.1 Why custom Hooks matter in large applications
Imagine that several application components need to:
Duplicating the same logic inside several components creates maintenance problems.
Custom Hooks allow developers to extract and reuse stateful logic.
A custom Hook is a function whose name starts with use and which can call React Hooks.
7.3 Custom Hooks share logic, not automatically state
Each component receives its own instance of the Hook's internal state.
They do not automatically share a single counter value.
To share the actual state, use:
A common parent with lifted state.
React explicitly distinguishes reusable Hook logic from shared application state. (React)
We can create a reusable Hook to track network status.
Note that browser online status indicates connection status reported by the browser, not guaranteed access to your application's server.
A large application may display hundreds of records.
Instead of implementing pagination repeatedly, create a Hook.
The generic type allows the same Hook to work with courses, tasks, students, and other collections.
Clean up external subscriptions when necessary.
Avoid building enormous Hooks that manage every part of an application.
The official React guidance recommends extracting concrete, reusable behavioural logic rather than inventing generic lifecycle wrappers. (React)
Practical exercise: Create usePagination, useOnlineStatus, useLocalStorage, and useToggle Hooks. Reuse them across multiple dashboard pages.
In a real frontend application, users need to move between different pages.
A traditional website may request a new HTML document from the server whenever the user navigates to another page.
A React single-page application (SPA) can instead use client-side routing.
The browser URL changes, React Router matches the new URL, and the appropriate component is displayed.
The application can retain shared layouts and state while navigating.
React Router: A routing library that connects application URLs with React components and navigation behaviour.
Route-level loading and data capabilities in supported modes.
React Router currently supports Declarative, Data, and Framework modes. In this module, we will primarily use Declarative Mode to understand basic routing and component architecture. (React Router)
For the current React Router v7 declarative setup:
Note: Older React Router v6 projects commonly use react-router-dom. Follow the import conventions for the installed major version rather than mixing examples from different versions.
The BrowserRouter component provides browser-based routing using the History API.
The BrowserRouter makes routing functionality available to its descendants.
Now each URL corresponds to a different component.
React Router provides two important navigation components.
Link — Used to navigate between routes.
NavLink — Useful when the application needs to display an active navigation state.
NavLink provides active-state information that can be used for styling.
Sometimes the application needs to navigate without a user clicking a link.
For example, after successfully logging in, the user should be redirected to the dashboard.
Use ordinary Link or NavLink elements for normal user-initiated navigation. Programmatic navigation is useful for actions such as successful form submission or logout. (React Router)
Client-side routing uses browser history to support navigation.
push: Add a new history entry.
replace: Replace the current history entry.
back: Return to the previous entry.
forward: Move to the next entry.
This replaces the current history entry rather than adding another one.
Navigation | Usually without full document reload | Often loads a new document
Shared interface | Can remain mounted | Often recreated per document
Backend involvement | Depends on architecture | Central to document delivery

An important deployment consideration: when someone directly opens /dashboard or refreshes that URL, the hosting server must be configured to serve the SPA entry point for supported client-side routes.
Otherwise, the browser may receive a server-side 404 even though navigation from the application's homepage works.
Practical exercise: Create a five-page React application with React Router. Add a Navbar, Sidebar, active navigation indicators, and browser back/forward support.

sections.title: Nested Routes, Dynamic Routes and Route Parameters

blocks.text: Large applications often contain pages that share a common layout.
Each page belongs to the same dashboard.
The dashboard layout should remain visible while the page content changes.
The parent component needs to indicate where child route content should appear.
React Router provides the Outlet component.
The Outlet renders the currently matched child route.
This allows the Navbar and Sidebar to remain part of the common layout.
An index route represents the default child page of a parent route.

<Route path="/dashboard" element={<DashboardLayout />}>
  <Route index element={<DashboardHome />} />
  <Route path="courses" element={<Courses />} />
</Route>
The index route is displayed when the user visits:
Sometimes a URL needs to contain an identifier.
For example, each course should have its own details page.
Instead of creating a separate route for every course, use a dynamic parameter.
The :courseId segment represents a dynamic route parameter.
React Router provides the useParams() Hook.
An important point: route parameters are strings, even when they represent numbers.
Validate or convert them before using them as numeric IDs.
A learning platform may have routes like:
These can be represented using nested dynamic routes.

<Route path="/courses/:courseId" element={<CourseLayout />}>
  <Route index element={<CourseOverview />} />
  <Route path="modules/:moduleId" element={<ModuleDetails />} />
  <Route
    path="modules/:moduleId/lessons/:lessonId"
    element={<LessonPage />}
  />
</Route>
The parent layout can display the course navigation while the specific module or lesson changes.
This generates the appropriate course details URL.
Users may enter an invalid URL.
A catch-all route can display a custom not-found page.
This prevents users from seeing an empty page when they visit an unknown frontend route.
React Router's nested routing system renders child content through Outlet and supports nested dynamic route structures. (React Router)
Practical exercise: Build a course navigation system with nested course, module, and lesson pages. Use dynamic parameters to retrieve the correct information for each URL.
Some pages should only be accessible to authenticated users.
A React application can use authentication state to decide which interface a user should see.
Expired session | Login or session-expired interface
It is important to distinguish checking a user's interface state from actually securing backend information.
The provider should retrieve or restore the user's authenticated session using the application's real authentication system.
For demonstration, the following provider shows the data structure:
A production implementation must connect this to actual session validation, login, logout, and session restoration.
This checks whether the application currently recognizes an authenticated user.

<Routes>
  <Route path="/login" element={<Login />} />
  <Route element={<ProtectedRoute />}>
    <Route path="/dashboard" element={<DashboardLayout />}>
      <Route index element={<DashboardHome />} />
      <Route path="courses" element={<MyCourses />} />
      <Route path="profile" element={<Profile />} />
    </Route>
  </Route>
</Routes>
The protected route acts as a parent wrapper.
Unauthenticated users are redirected to login.
Some applications support multiple user roles.
A role-aware route can check permissions before displaying a protected interface.
Now administration routes can be placed inside this route group.
After a successful login, navigate to the dashboard.
A complete login implementation should also preserve the intended destination when appropriate and validate the authentication response.
10.8 Critical security distinction: frontend versus backend protection
This is one of the most important topics in professional frontend engineering.
A protected React route is not a security boundary.
A user can inspect frontend code, modify browser state, or directly send requests to backend endpoints.
React route protection controls which interface is displayed. Backend authorization controls which information and operations the user is actually allowed to access.
For example, even if an administrator page is hidden from students, the backend must still verify administrator permissions before allowing administrative API requests.
React Router's documentation also warns that authentication checks in a parent route alone do not automatically secure independently executed child loaders and actions. (React Router)
Practical exercise: Create a student dashboard and administrator dashboard with different route access. Implement session loading, login redirects, logout, and backend authorization checks.
A layout route provides a shared interface structure for multiple pages.
Each group may require a different navigation system.
Instead of repeating the layout in every page, create reusable layouts.

Application
├── PublicLayout
│   ├── Home
│   ├── Login
│   └── Registration
├── StudentLayout
│   ├── Dashboard
│   ├── Courses
│   ├── Assignments
│   └── Profile
└── AdminLayout
    ├── AdminDashboard
    ├── UserManagement
    └── CourseManagement
The layout contains the shared structure.
The Outlet displays the currently active page.
The administrator can have a different design and navigation system.

<Routes>
  <Route element={<PublicLayout />}>
    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
    <Route path="/login" element={<Login />} />
  </Route>
  <Route element={<ProtectedRoute />}>
    <Route path="/dashboard" element={<StudentLayout />}>
      <Route index element={<DashboardHome />} />
      <Route path="courses" element={<MyCourses />} />
      <Route path="assignments" element={<Assignments />} />
      <Route path="profile" element={<Profile />} />
    </Route>
  </Route>
</Routes>
11.5 What is a layout route without a URL segment?
React Router supports pathless layout routes.
The parent wrapper does not add a URL segment.
It only introduces a shared route-level structure or condition.
A larger application should centralize navigation definitions where practical.
The Sidebar can filter navigation items based on the authenticated user.
However, hiding links for unauthorized users is only a user-interface decision. Backend permission checks remain mandatory.
Common elements are maintained in several places.
With layout routes, the shared structure is maintained in one place.
React Router supports pathless layouts and nested layouts using its routing tree. (React Router)
Practical exercise: Build public, student, and administrator layouts. Each should have its own Navbar and navigation structure, with nested child routes.
If all these components are included in the initial JavaScript bundle, the browser may need to download a large amount of code before the application becomes usable.
However, a student visiting the homepage does not necessarily need the administrator dashboard or assignment editor immediately.
Code splitting divides a large application bundle into smaller chunks.
Instead of loading all application code together, the application can load different parts when needed.

Initial Application Bundle
├── App
├── Shared Components
├── Basic Layout
└── Routing

Additional Chunks
├── Dashboard
├── Courses
├── Assignments
├── Analytics
└── Administration
This can reduce the amount of JavaScript required during initial page loading.
Unlike static imports, dynamic imports can load modules on demand.
They return a Promise that resolves with the imported module.
Bundlers such as Vite can use these imports as code-splitting boundaries.
React provides lazy() to load a component only when React first needs to render it.
Now the Analytics component's module can be loaded on demand.
The imported module should provide a default component export for this form.
A lazily loaded component may take some time to download.
React provides Suspense to display a fallback during loading.
While the component code is loading, React displays the fallback.
When it becomes available, React displays the actual component.
One of the most useful applications is lazy loading individual pages.
Each page can be placed into a separate asynchronous module chunk by the build tool.
12.7 Understanding lazy loading versus normal loading
Imported module is included in the normal dependency graph | Module can be downloaded on demand
Usually available in the initial application bundle | Can be loaded later
Simple for small components | Useful for large page-level modules
No separate loading fallback is inherently needed | Usually paired with Suspense
12.8 When should lazy loading be used?
Avoid lazy loading every tiny button or label.
Too many small chunks can introduce additional network overhead and complexity.
The React documentation describes combining lazy() and Suspense to load components when they are first rendered. (React)
Practical exercise: Convert a multi-page React application to use lazy-loaded routes. Compare its initial bundle size before and after code splitting.

sections.title: Suspense, Error Boundaries and Fallback Interfaces

blocks.text: Modern frontend applications depend on several external and internal systems.
A route may still be loading.
A component module may not have downloaded.
A component may throw an unexpected rendering error.
A data-fetching system may enter an error state.
A professional application should not leave users staring at a blank screen.
It should display a meaningful fallback interface.
Suspense allows React to display fallback content when a supported child suspends during rendering.
When the Reports module has not finished loading, React displays the fallback.
Once the component is ready, React displays it.
A fallback can be any valid React node.
You can also use skeleton interfaces:
A skeleton can provide a visual representation of the content that will appear.
13.4 Important distinction: Suspense does not catch every asynchronous operation
Suspense does not automatically display its fallback whenever an ordinary fetch() request inside useEffect is pending.
This operation does not automatically activate Suspense.
Suspense supports specific mechanisms, including lazy-loaded components and Suspense-compatible data sources.
Use ordinary loading and error state management for normal Fetch operations unless you are using a compatible data-fetching architecture.
An Error Boundary is a React component that catches certain errors thrown while rendering its descendant component tree.
It displays alternative UI rather than allowing the affected section to break the entire application.
For example, imagine that the Analytics component contains a rendering bug.
Without an appropriate boundary, the error can affect the surrounding application interface.
With an Error Boundary, you can isolate that section.
React currently exposes Error Boundary functionality through class-component lifecycle APIs.
If a descendant throws an applicable rendering error, the boundary displays its fallback.
13.7 What Error Boundaries do not catch
Error Boundaries do not automatically catch errors from:
These errors require their appropriate error-handling mechanisms.
For example, asynchronous API failures should generally be handled using try/catch and application error state.
React's documentation explains these limitations and the Error Boundary lifecycle APIs. (React)
A production-style page can use both mechanisms.
Suspense handles the loading period for supported suspended content.
Error Boundary handles applicable rendering failures.
For more advanced applications, libraries such as react-error-boundary provide convenient APIs for reusable error handling.
Component rendering error | Error Boundary fallback
API request failure | Error message and retry
The user should understand what happened and what action they can take.

Practical exercise: Add Suspense boundaries around lazy-loaded dashboard routes and Error Boundaries around individual application sections. Intentionally create a component rendering error and verify that the rest of the dashboard remains accessible.
A React application may work correctly but still feel slow.
Navigating between pages takes too long.
Too many components render during an interaction.
Large JavaScript bundles delay initial loading.
These problems become increasingly important as applications grow.

Dashboard
├── Navbar
├── Sidebar
├── CourseList
│   ├── CourseCard
│   ├── CourseCard
│   └── CourseCard
└── Footer
If the Dashboard manages unrelated state, updates can lead to more components rendering than necessary.
A good architecture keeps transient state close to the components that need it.
React provides memo() to allow React to skip rendering a component when its props are unchanged.
If the parent renders again but these props remain the same, React may skip rendering the memoized component.
By default, React compares individual props using Object.is.
This is an optimization, not a guarantee that the component will never render again.
A new object is created during every parent render.
Even when the object contains identical information, it has a different reference.
That can reduce the effectiveness of memoization.
But only introduce this optimization when it provides a measurable benefit.
A frequent architectural mistake is placing every state variable at the top of the application.
For example, a single App component might hold:
Then many descendants can render whenever shared state changes.
Instead, place state close to the components that need it.
This reduces unnecessary communication and simplifies the architecture.
Consider a dashboard displaying 20,000 student records.
Rendering every row simultaneously can create unnecessary DOM nodes and performance problems.
List virtualization solves this by rendering only the visible portion of the list.
For example, if a table displays 20,000 records, the browser might render only the records currently visible in the viewport plus a small buffer.
This technique is particularly useful for:
Consider a search field that triggers expensive filtering or an API request on every keystroke.
The application could generate many unnecessary requests.
Debouncing waits until the user stops typing for a specified period.

const [search, setSearch] = useState("");
const debouncedSearch = useDebouncedValue(search, 300);
The application can now perform expensive filtering or server searches using debouncedSearch.
For network search, also consider cancelling outdated requests.
Do not optimize based only on assumptions.
Use React Developer Tools and its Profiler to understand:
Which components take the most time.
Whether memoization actually improves the experience.
React also provides the Profiler component for programmatic performance measurements.
The callback provides information about the committed rendering work.
Performance results should be measured in realistic production-like conditions, because development mode can introduce additional work.
Keep state local | Reduce unnecessary update propagation
Code splitting | Reduce initial JavaScript bundle
Lazy loading | Load features when needed
Modern React also provides React Compiler, which can automatically perform many memoization optimizations when configured and compatible with the project.
This means developers should understand useMemo, useCallback, and memo, but should not assume every application requires manual memoization everywhere. (React)

Practical exercise: Create a dashboard containing a large collection of courses. Profile the application, introduce search debouncing, memoize expensive computations where necessary, and compare performance.

sections.title: Organizing Large React Applications and Feature-Based Architecture

blocks.text: Consider an application that has been developed for six months.
If everything is stored in a few large folders, locating and maintaining functionality becomes difficult.
A scalable folder structure provides a logical organization.
A common organization separates files by technical responsibility.

src/
├── components/

Each feature contains the files related to its functionality.
A feature should represent a meaningful application capability.
Auth | Login, registration, session and permissions
Courses | Course catalogue, enrollment and details
Progress | Lesson completion and learning statistics
Each feature should own its specific business logic where practical.
Shared functionality belongs in the shared directory.
Not every component needs to be globally reusable.
A component should be moved into a shared directory when there is a genuine cross-feature reuse requirement.
Do not create a shared component simply because two components look somewhat similar.

The component should not need to know all the low-level details of how the backend works.
It should call a suitable feature Hook or service.
The Hook manages the application-facing data logic.
The API service handles network communication.
This makes each layer easier to maintain and test.
Large applications benefit from predictable import paths.
Path aliases such as @/ can be configured in TypeScript and Vite.
This reduces long relative paths and makes files easier to navigate.
Feature-based architecture can support several engineering goals:
For a very large organization, architecture may also be divided into separate packages or applications.
However, a modular monolithic React application is often a sensible starting point.
You do not need micro-frontends or dozens of separate packages just because the application is large.
Give every feature a clear responsibility.
Keep shared UI components independent of specific business logic.
Keep state close to its consumers unless sharing is required.
Keep API communication separate from display code when practical.
Introduce abstractions only when they improve maintainability.
Organize around the application's actual functionality rather than theoretical complexity.

Practical exercise: Take a React application with at least five major features and reorganize it into a feature-based architecture. Ensure that imports, routes, components, Hooks, and services continue to work.

Phase 1 — Application foundation: Configure React, TypeScript, Vite, project folders, shared types, and application providers.
Phase 2 — Component architecture: Build reusable Navbar, Sidebar, cards, tables, buttons, notification components, and dashboard widgets.
Phase 3 — State management: Implement Context, useReducer, authentication state, course data, assignments, and notifications.
Phase 4 — Routing architecture: Implement public and protected routes, nested pages, route parameters, navigation layouts, and not-found handling.
Phase 5 — Backend integration: Connect the dashboard to APIs and implement request handling, validation, loading states, and error handling.
Phase 6 — Performance: Implement lazy loading, Suspense, profiling, search debouncing, and justified memoization.
Phase 7 — Testing and completion: Verify route navigation, shared state updates, authorization, component failures, responsiveness, and production builds.
The finished application must be tested for:
Correct course IDs in dynamic routes.
Authentication | Protected interface and authorization integration
Performance | Lazy loading and measured optimization
Error handling | Suspense and Error Boundaries
